newsitem.title: UK: IRA hospital attack puts Protestant truce at risk.
newsitem.headline: IRA hospital attack puts Protestant truce at risk.

text.p: A leading pro-British politician warned on Saturday that the IRA guerrilla shooting of a policeman inside a children's hospital could lead Protestant Loyalist foes to end a two-year truce and strike back.

"My belief is that it is an attempt to provoke Loyalists to retaliate. My fear is that it is more likely than not that they will succeed," David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of the banned Protestant Ulster Volunteer Force, told Reuters.

Irish Republican Army gunmen, opposed to British rule of Northern Ireland, opened fire on a police bodyguard who was in a corridor while a prominent Protestant politician and his wife visited their seven-year-old son in a Belfast hospital on Friday.
The policeman escaped with slight injuries and the IRA in a statement denied it had intended to assassinate Nigel Dodds -- the Protestant political leader who was being guarded.
The incident, which security sources said was the first acknowledged IRA shooting attack since the guerrillas relaunched a bombing war nine months ago, has deepened gloom in the volatile province.
Four shots were fired in the attack, the police said. One hit an empty baby incubator.

Northern Ireland's police chief Ronnie Flanagan said the attack showed an "absolute and total disregard for human life. To strike where children are gravely ill and already in traumatic circumstances is appalling."
Ervine said on BBC radio that Northern Ireland was staring into an abyss.
The October 1994 truce by Protestant guerrillas has held despite an IRA bomb attack on British military headquarters near Belfast in October in which one soldier died.
"It is obvious to loyalism that the IRA is cranking up its war machine," Ervine said.
"I think that people like myself who have constantly argued that a democratic path must be followed...I fear, rather, that we are likely to be marginalised certainly for the forseeable future."
Mitchell McLaughlin, chairman of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, described the shooting as terrible but declined to condemn it.

McLaughlin, who said Loyalist gunmen had killed the vice-president of his party, Maire Drumm, in a hospital bed in Belfast more than 10 years ago, said Sinn Fein should be allowed into all-party peace talks.
"These terrible events can only be prevented when we come up with a negotiated settlement. That is what we (Sinn Fein) are bending our efforts to," he told BBC radio.
Britain and Ireland say Sinn Fein will not have a place in talks until the IRA calls a fresh ceasefire.
British Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday that even if the IRA continued its violence for a further 50 years, Britain would not let them to bomb their way into talks.
